en.title: The Tower of Babel

passage.a: People who speak the same language start building a city and a very tall tower. Then God confuses their language. They can no longer understand one another, so they stop building and spread out across the earth. The story gives us something to think about: working together takes understanding.
passage.b: People who share one language decide to build a city and a tower reaching toward the sky. They want to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. God confuses their language, and the builders can no longer understand one another. The work stops, and the people spread across the earth.
passage.c: The builders of Babel share a language, a plan, and the wish to make a name for themselves. They build a city and a tower, hoping to remain together. God confuses their language; construction stops, and they are scattered. The account links the name Babel with the confusion of language, inviting questions about ambition, shared purpose, and the limits of unity.

en.title: Abram’s Journey to Canaan

passage.a: Abram, who is later named Abraham, sets out for a new land. His wife Sarai, later named Sarah, travels with him, along with his nephew Lot and their household. They reach Canaan. Later, God tells Abram to look at the stars and promises him many descendants. The journey and the stars are two clues to Abraham's story.
passage.b: God calls Abram to leave his homeland and go to a land he will be shown. Abram leaves Haran with Sarai, his nephew Lot, and their household, and they reach Canaan. Later, God points him toward the stars with a promise of countless descendants. These are separate moments in one story. At this stage, Abraham and Sarah are still called Abram and Sarai.
passage.c: At seventy-five, Abram leaves Haran in response to God's call, traveling with Sarai, Lot, and their household to Canaan. The departure in Genesis 12 and the promise of descendants pictured through the stars in Genesis 15 are distinct moments. Together they connect an uncertain journey with a promised future. Abram and Sarai receive the names Abraham and Sarah later in the narrative.

en.title: Jacob’s Dream

passage.a: Jacob stops to sleep while traveling. He places a stone near his head. In a dream, he sees a ladder reaching from the earth toward heaven, with angels going up and down. When he wakes, he gives the place a new name: Bethel.
passage.b: On his way from Beersheba to Haran, Jacob stops for the night and places a stone near his head. He dreams of a ladder, or stairway, joining earth and heaven, with angels moving up and down. God promises to be with him. When Jacob wakes, he recognizes new meaning in the place and names it Bethel.
passage.c: Traveling from Beersheba toward Haran, Jacob spends the night on the road with a stone near his head. His dream joins earth and heaven through a ladder or stairway, with angels ascending and descending. God's promise of presence turns an ordinary stopping place into a remembered encounter. Jacob names it Bethel; the town had previously been called Luz.

en.title: Joseph’s Dreams

passage.a: Joseph tells his family about two dreams. In the first, his brothers' bundles of grain bow down to his bundle. In the second, the sun, moon, and eleven stars bow down to him. His brothers become jealous. Their father questions Joseph about the dream but keeps it in mind.
passage.b: Joseph shares two dreams with his family. First, his brothers' bundles of grain bow to his own. Then the sun, moon, and eleven stars bow to him. His brothers hear a claim that he will rule over them, and their resentment grows. His father rebukes him but keeps the matter in mind. The dreams add to an already strained family relationship.
passage.c: Joseph's dreams turn familiar images of work and the sky into unsettling pictures of authority. His brothers' sheaves bow to his sheaf; later, the sun, moon, and eleven stars bow to him. The brothers resent the implication of rule and are jealous. Jacob rebukes Joseph while keeping the matter in mind, a response more complicated than either simple approval or dismissal.
